title: C-F bond integration in polymeric carbon nitride enables oxygen-tolerant photocatalytic reduction of NO to N_2

paper_content.abstract: The selective photocatalytic decomposition of NO under oxygen-rich conditions presents a significant challenge, largely due to the preferential reduction of O2 over NO. To overcome this limitation, we develop an F-modified polymeric carbon nitride catalyst (e-FCN). Under visible light irradiation in simulated ambient air (20% O2), the e-FCN catalyst achieves 85% NO conversion with 92% selectivity toward N2. It exhibits high apparent quantum yields for N2 formation (29.1% at 365 nm and ≥9.9% between 405 and 465 nm) and maintains its performance over 12 consecutive cycles without deactivation. Mechanistic investigations indicate that the incorporation of a C–F bond suppresses the detrimental C=O formation from O2 activation, thereby passivating the catalyst toward O2. Concurrently, e-FCN selectively adsorbs NO and promotes N–N coupling between adjacent NO molecules, ultimately converting NO to N2 via an N2O intermediate. This synergy of selective NO adsorption and controlled decomposition enables selective and oxygen-tolerant photocatalytic NO decomposition.
paper_content.introduction:
The combustion of fossil fuels and vehicle emissions represent the primary sources of increasing nitrogen oxides (NOx) emissions. These NO compounds, with NO constituting approximately 95% of the total, exert significant detrimental effects on the environment and ecosystems1–3, which contribute to acid rain, greenhouse effect, photochemical smog, and secondary ultrafine particulate matter formation4,5. Currently, selective catalytic reduction (SCR) stands as the most established technology for NOx reduction. SCR employs a chemical reductant such as H2 or NH3 at temperatures exceeding 200°C6,7. Despite its effectiveness, post-SCR exhaust may contain several tens of ppmv NO. In indoor or urban environments, NO concentrations may be diluted to ppbv or several ppmv levels. However, these levels often still exceed the emission limits stipulated by the World Health Organization8,9. Additionally, SCR technology encounters challenges in removing low-concentration NO, highlighting the need for alternative methods to achieve effective elimination10,11. While the adsorption method can remove low-concentration NO, it carries the risk of generating N2O and NO2 through NO disproportionation, thereby contributing to secondary environmental pollution12,13. Another approach, photocatalytic oxidation of NO to NO3−, has been proposed as a promising technology for NO removal in indoor or urban settings14–16. Nonetheless, this method unavoidably generates more toxic NO2 as a byproduct, and the resulting nonvolatile NO3− species may accumulate and occupy surface active sites, leading to the deactivation of the photocatalyst17.

N2 could potentially be formed as another product of photocatalytic NO conversion. The inherent advantage of N2 as a non-toxic and non-adsorbing gas helps mitigate concerns about catalyst deactivation and secondary environmental impact18. Under ambient air conditions, the Gibbs free energy changes for the reduction of O2 to superoxide radical (•O2−) and hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) are 3 kJ·mol−1 and 117 kJ·mol−1, respectively19,20. These values are significantly lower than the energy required to cleave the N=O bond (607 kJ·mol−1) and form the N≡N bond (946 kJ·mol−1)21, both of which are necessary for the reduction of NO to N2. Consequently, the activation of O2 to form •O2− and H2O2 is thermodynamically favored. The resulting reactive oxygen species (•O2− and H2O2) should promote the oxidation of NO to NO3−, thereby inhibiting the reduction of NO to N2. Consequently, achieving selective photocatalytic reduction of NO in the presence of O2 remains a significant challenge.

Most works on photocatalytic NO decomposition have typically been carried out under anoxic conditions to minimize the influence of O2 22. While some studies have observed trace amounts of N2 in the presence of O2 23–25, NO decomposition to N2 in air conditioning is strongly hindered. Similarly, the photocatalytic reduction of CO2 in the presence of O2, akin to photocatalytic NO reduction, presents a formidable challenge. Recent efforts have therefore concentrated on incorporating CO2 adsorption sites into catalyst structures to lower local O2 concentrations and enable in situ CO2 capture and concentration26–31. Expanding on these methodologies, it is imperative to develop catalysts customized for the selective adsorption and decomposition of NO in the presence of O2.

Density functional theory (DFT) computations indicate that introducing a C–F bond into the polymeric carbon nitride (CN) model induces surface charge polarization around the F modification site. This polarization facilitates the selective adsorption of NO in the presence of O2 32. However, there are currently no experimental evidence supporting the selective adsorption of NO by F-modified CN in the presence of O2. In situ observations have revealed an unexpected accumulation of C=O groups on CN due to surface carbon oxidation during the oxygen evolution reaction (OER) in the water splitting process, leading to the deactivation of CN catalyst33. To address this issue, a surface fluorination strategy has been developed to mitigate the C=O accumulation by forming a C–F bond and to decrease OER barriers through the activation of adjacent N reactive sites. This approach significantly enhances the overall water-splitting efficiency of F-modified CN under visible light33. These findings propose the hypothesis that the introduction of the C–F bond in the CN structure should enable the selective NO adsorption capability while reducing interaction with O2.

Our prepared F-modified carbon nitride (e-FCN)34 enables oxygen-tolerant, selective photoreduction of NO to N2 under visible light. In contrast, O-modified carbon nitride (e-OCN)35 favors the activation of O2, shifting the reaction toward NO oxidation. This demonstrates that e-FCN uniquely possesses the capacity to preferentially adsorb and reduce NO even in O2, presenting a pioneering approach for selective NO reduction to N2 in oxygen-rich environments.
paper_content.results:
Preparation and characterization of CN-based catalysts
The preparation of CN-based catalysts is illustrated in Fig. 1A. The bulk-OCN and bulk-FCN were synthesized by incorporating glycolic acid and NH4F, respectively, via the traditional condensation process34,35, followed by thermal exfoliation to produce e-OCN and e-FCN36. For comparison, bulk-CN and e-CN were prepared via melamine pyrolysis without additives. X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis (Fig. S1A) revealed two characteristic peaks at 13.0° and 27.4°, corresponding to the (100) and (002) crystallographic planes, which are indicative of in-plane tri-s-triazine units and interlayer stacking, respectively37. A notable broadening of these peaks in the exfoliated catalysts suggests a reduction in crystallite size36. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) confirmed successful exfoliation, showing a decrease in average particle thickness from 40.1–48.2 nm for the bulk catalysts to 2.3–4.9 nm for the exfoliated catalysts (Fig. S2). Based on a theoretical monolayer thickness of 0.325 nm for CN38, this corresponds to a reduction from approximately 124–148 layers to merely 7–15 layers. This finding was corroborated by dynamic light scattering (DLS), which showed a substantial decrease in the average hydrodynamic diameter from approximately 900 nm to 120 nm post-exfoliation (Fig. S3). Collectively, these results confirm the successful exfoliation of the bulk CN (bulk CN)-based catalysts. Both AFM and DLS revealed a consistent exfoliation trend across the catalyst series. AFM measurements indicated that the particle thickness decreased in the order (Fig. S2): e-CN (4.3–4.9 nm) > e-OCN (2.8–3.4 nm) > e-FCN (2.3–2.7 nm). This trend was corroborated by DLS, which showed a corresponding decrease in hydrodynamic diameter (Fig. S3): e-CN (133.1±1.7 nm) > e-OCN (122.7±1.3 nm) > e-FCN (110.6±1.1 nm). Charge distribution calculations confirmed the strong electron-withdrawing nature of the O and F atoms, which generated a highly positive C center (Fig. S4). The greater electronegativity of F resulted in a more positive charge on this C center in the FCN model (+1.81) compared with that in the OCN model (+1.70). We therefore propose that this electron-withdrawing effect is the primary driver of enhanced exfoliation. The incorporation of O or F into the CN matrix attenuates the interlayer π-π interactions, thereby facilitating delamination. The pronounced efficacy of F stems directly from its higher electronegativity, which more effectively disrupts these cohesive forces and promotes exfoliation.

Solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy of 13C, 1H, and 19F (solid-state 13C, 1H, and 19F NMR) was employed to probe chemical environments (Fig. 1B–D). The 13C NMR spectra (Fig. 1B) showed consistent peaks at 156.4 ppm (C3N) and 164.8 ppm (C2N-NHx), confirming structural integrity39. For e-CN, a shoulder peak was observed at 162.9 ppm, which is assigned to the C2N-NH structure formed during the thermal exfoliation of bulk-CN40. This peak disappeared upon the introduction of electron-withdrawing O/F. We attribute this disappearance to a strong inductive effect from the O/F modifiers. The carbon atom in the C2N-NH structure is situated closer to the modification site than the carbon in the C2N-NHx structure (whose signal appears at 164.8 ppm). Consequently, the inductive effect induces a downfield shift of the C2N-NH signal, causing it to merge with the adjacent peak at 164.8 ppm and become unresolvable. 1H NMR (Fig. 1C) revealed peaks at 4.2 ppm (–NH2) and 9.4 ppm (–NH–), with an additional peak at 7.2 ppm (–OH) in e-OCN, verifying O modification41. The 19F NMR spectrum of e-FCN (Fig. 1D) exhibited a distinct peak at −145.5 ppm, confirming C–F bonding42.

X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis (Fig. S1B–D) corroborated these findings. The C 1s spectra displayed peaks at 284.8 eV (C–C), 286.4 eV (C–M, M=NH, OH, F), and 288.2 eV (N–C=N)39,41, while N 1s spectra showed contributions from N-C (398.6 eV), N-C3 (399.3 eV), and NHx (400.8 eV)39. The O 1s spectra (Fig. 1C) featured two typical peaks for all three catalysts: one at 533.1 eV (O–H from adsorbed H2O)43 and another at 532.0 eV (C–O–C). While the C–O–C signal in e-CN and e-FCN originates solely from adsorbed CO2 43, in e-OCN it has a dual origin from both structural O modifiers41 and adsorbed CO2 43. Furthermore, e-OCN is distinctive in exhibiting an additional –OH peak at 530.9 eV41. The F 1s spectrum of e-FCN (Fig. 1D) exhibited a peak at 687.3 eV, further verifying C–F bonding42,44. Electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) spectroscopy (Fig. 1E) revealed a Lorentzian peak (g=2.005) in all catalysts except bulk-CN, attributed to unpaired electrons in graphitic rings45,46. Exfoliated catalysts showed enhanced signals (e-FCN > e-OCN > e-CN), indicating EPR increased defect density, whereas bulk catalysts exhibited weaker signals. In particular, bulk-CN exhibited no detectable EPR signal. These results demonstrate that O and F modifications introduce –OH and C–F moieties, respectively, which may influence photocatalytic activity in NO decomposition.

Photocatalytic NO conversion behaviors of modified CN catalysts
The comparative evaluation of photocatalytic NO decomposition in a 20% O2 atmosphere (simulating ambient air) was conducted using e-CN, e-OCN, and e-FCN in a continuous flow reactor under 425 nm light irradiation. To clearly present the catalytic reaction conditions, this study systematically summarized all relevant experimental parameters in Table S1. This consolidated table improved the logical organization of data presentation while enhancing the accessibility and clarity of the manuscript. As shown in Fig. 2A, significant differences are observed in NO removal efficiency among the catalysts: e-CN (20%), e-OCN (68%), and e-FCN (85%). Table S2 summarized the concentrations of N-containing products after 30 min of reaction over the three catalysts. In all cases, the total N concentration, which was calculated as the sum of all N-containing products, matched the initial NO concentration, meeting the N balance throughout the reaction. The data in Table S2 also revealed that N2 was the dominant product in NO decomposition over e-FCN, whereas N2O and NO3− were the primary products over e-CN and e-OCN. Based on these results, the product selectivity at 30 min was determined, demonstrating that e-FCN exhibited significantly higher N2 selectivity (92%) compared with e-CN (1%) and e-OCN (7%). Notably, e-OCN showed higher NO3− selectivity (55%) than e-CN (46%).

To identify the N source in N2 formation, isotopic labeling experiments were conducted using a 4% 15NO gas mixture in 20% O2/Ar within a sealed reactor. The system was rigorously prepared through multiple evacuation and purging cycles to ensure atmospheric integrity. Control pre-reaction analysis by GC-MS (Fig. S5A) confirmed the absence of N2 contamination, as only a characteristic O2 peak was observed in both the GC trace and the corresponding MS spectrum. Following a 2-h photocatalytic reaction, GC-MS analysis demonstrated that the N2 produced originated exclusively from the decomposition of 15NO, as indicated by the sole detection of 15N2 (Fig. 2B). A separate experiment was performed to ascertain the origin of the co-generated O2, utilizing a mixture of 4% NO in 20% 18O2/Ar. Control pre-reaction GC-MS analysis (Fig. S5B) confirmed the presence of exclusively 18O2, ruling out significant O2 contamination. After the photocatalytic reaction, the MS spectrum of O2 (Fig. 2C) revealed a composite signal for 16O2 and 18O2. The absence of a peak at m/z = 34 (16O18O) indicates that isotopic exchange between oxygen atoms did not occur. The experimental 16O2:18O2 ratio was approximately 1:11, which aligns accurately with the theoretically predicted ratio of 1:10.7 based on reaction selectivity. This result confirms that the newly generated O2 originates from the decomposition of NO.

To accurately quantify the N2 and O2 products, photocatalytic NO decomposition was conducted in an Ar atmosphere to eliminate interference from O2 (Fig. S6). As shown in Fig. S6C, e-FCN decomposed NO into nearly equimolar amounts of N2 and O2, consistent with previous reports17,25,47. Figures 2A and S6D revealed that the three catalysts exhibited similar N2 selectivity under both Ar and 20% O2/Ar atmospheres, despite following fundamentally different reaction pathways. Under the Ar atmosphere, e-CN, e-OCN, and e-FCN all underwent photocatalytic NO decomposition, producing N2O as a byproduct. In contrast, under the 20% O2/Ar atmosphere, the catalysts displayed distinct behaviors: e-FCN remained primarily governed by NO decomposition, with minimal NO oxidation, resulting in comparable N2 selectivity in both conditions. However, as shown in Fig. 2A, e-CN and e-OCN generated substantially more NO3− than N2O, indicating a predominant photocatalytic oxidation pathway (converting NO to NO3−) rather than decomposition. These differences underscore the selective catalytic preference for specific reaction pathways in the presence of O2.

The catalyst surface temperature was monitored using a thermocouple. As shown in Fig. S7A, the temperature increased from 25°C to 35°C during the photocatalytic reaction and stabilized thereafter, indicating that the LED light source did not induce significant heating of the catalyst. To exclude thermal contributions to NO decomposition, a control experiment was performed at 35°C in the absence of light. Figure S7B shows that all catalysts exhibited negligible activity under these conditions, confirming that NO decomposition was exclusively photocatalytic rather than thermally driven. To investigate the correlation between the initial NH4F amount and the F/C atomic ratio in the e-FCN catalyst, we first conducted quantitative elemental analysis of C, N, and F in e-FCN catalysts prepared with varying NH4F amounts. Based on the elemental composition data (Table S3), the corresponding F/C atomic ratios were calculated. As illustrated in Fig. S8A, a strong linear relationship (R2=0.9933) was observed between the initial NH4F amount and the F/C atomic ratio, demonstrating that the F content in e-FCN can be precisely tuned by adjusting the initial NH4F amount. Further analysis of the influence of F/C atomic ratios on catalytic performance (Fig. S8B) revealed that the e-FCN catalyst exhibited optimal activity at an F/C ratio of 0.10 at%. The process parameters, including catalyst mass and gas flow rate, were optimized to improve the photocatalytic NO decomposition efficiency (Figs. S9–10). Following this optimization, the apparent quantum yields (AQYs) for N2 formation were determined. As illustrated in Fig. 2D and Table S4, the AQYs of e-FCN are no lower than 9.9% within the 365–465 nm range, reaching a peak of 29.1% at 365 nm.

To evaluate the distinctiveness of the proposed C–F modification strategy, we systematically compared the performance of several catalysts under both Ar and 20% O2/Ar atmospheres. The tested catalysts included: e-FCN (containing C–F bonds), our previously developed mp-TiO2-x 25, surface-fluorinated F-mp-TiO2-x 48, and the BiOBr/BiOF system featuring O-Br/F bonds49. As shown in Fig. 3A, B, e-FCN exhibited pronounced catalytic performance under both conditions. Notably, while mp-TiO2-x demonstrated activity comparable to e-FCN in an Ar atmosphere, its NO removal efficiency and N2 selectivity decreased significantly in 20% O2/Ar, with substantial NO2 byproduct formation. Further analysis revealed that surface F doping (F-mp-TiO2-x) slightly improved NO removal efficiency but increased NO2 generation, suggesting that surface F doping primarily promotes the undesired oxidation of NO to NO2 rather than NO decomposition under oxygen-rich conditions. Similarly, the BiOF system (containing O–F bonds) showed marginally higher activity than BiOBr but remained ineffective for NO decomposition in an oxygen-rich environment. These comparative results clearly demonstrate the distinct advantage of the C–F modification strategy in developing highly efficient NO decomposition catalysts.

Although photocatalytic processes for NO removal have been extensively studied22, the majority of prior research has focused on the selective oxidation of NO to NO3−. We recently employed mp-TiO2-x to achieve selective NO reduction to N2 without a chemical reductant in anoxic conditions, but its performance was drastically reduced in the presence of O2 25. In contrast, e-FCN demonstrated pronounced efficiency in converting NO to N2 across a range of NO concentrations (0.5–2.0 ppmv; see Fig. 3C) and the concentration of O2 had a negligible effect on both NO removal efficiency and N2 selectivity (Fig. 3D). Conversely, oxygen-modified CN (e-OCN) promoted NO oxidation to NO3− in the presence of O2 (Fig. S11), shifting the primary byproduct from N2O to NO3− as O2 concentration increased from 0% to 20%. This behavior starkly contrasts with F-modified CN (e-FCN), which enables oxygen-tolerant NO decomposition to N2 regardless of O2 presence. As listed in Tables S5 and 6, e-FCN demonstrates competitive photocatalytic performance and AQYs for NO decomposition under 20% O2, even at an initial NO concentration as low as 0.5 ppmv, when compared with previously reported catalysts.

In durability tests, e-FCN demonstrated consistent NO removal efficiency and N2 selectivity over 12 consecutive cycles (Fig. 4A). In contrast, e-OCN exhibited a gradual decline in both NO removal efficiency and N2/NO3− selectivity (Fig. S12), with detectable NO2 formation emerging from the second cycle onward (Fig. S12B). Furthermore, measurements of accumulated NO3− on the catalyst surfaces revealed significantly higher deposition on e-OCN compared to e-FCN (Fig. 4B). These results suggest that e-OCN primarily oxidizes NO to NO3−, leading to catalyst deactivation via NO3− accumulation, whereas e-FCN predominantly decomposes NO into N2 and O2, minimizing NO3− generation and maintaining stable performance. Post-cycling characterization via XRD, solid-state NMR, and XPS (Fig. S13), along with elemental analysis (Table S3), confirmed the structural and compositional integrity of the e-FCN after 12 cycles.

As shown in Fig. 4C, e-FCN exhibited stable performance in both NO removal and N2 selectivity under continuous flow conditions over a 3-h period under RH=0% and constant light intensity. The catalyst surface temperature and the inlet gas flow rate were monitored in real time. Under irradiation from a 425 nm LED light source, the catalyst surface temperature showed no significant increase, remaining stable at approximately 35°C throughout the reaction (Fig. S14A). Concurrently, the gas flow rate at the reactor inlet remained constant without notable fluctuation (Fig. S14B). The NO removal efficiency and N2 selectivity fluctuated in response to changes in light intensity but remained generally stable under RH=45% (Fig. 4D). As previously demonstrated (Fig. S7B), thermal effects are negligible for NO decomposition at 35°C, eliminating temperature as a variable. Consequently, the observed performance fluctuations are primarily attributed to changes in light intensity, which directly modulate the yield of photogenerated charge carriers and thus the reaction kinetics within a certain range50.

In practical indoor environments, air contains a certain level of relative humidity (RH), and NO pollutants often coexist with other gases, such as CO2, NO2, and SO2 51. It is therefore essential to evaluate the effects of RH and coexisting gases on photocatalytic NO decomposition over e-FCN. Figures S15 and 16 systematically examined these influences by testing e-FCN under common indoor RH levels and typical concentration ratios of NO to CO2, NO2, and SO2. Figure S15 indicated that RH has a minor effect on photocatalytic NO decomposition, suggesting that H2O molecules do not significantly compete with NO for adsorption and activation sites on the catalyst surface. Similarly, coexisting CO2 exhibited a negligible impact (Fig. S16A, B). This observation aligns with prior theoretical calculations indicating that the adsorption energy of NO on F-CN is significantly more favorable than that of CO2, leading to the preferential adsorption of NO32. To evaluate the effect of NO2, the total initial NOx concentration was maintained at 2.0 ppmv while varying the NO2 proportion. The results indicate that neither the NOx removal efficiency nor the N2 selectivity was significantly affected (Fig. S16C, D). Furthermore, no NO2 was detected in the effluent. In this study, the initial NO concentration exceeded that of the coexisting NO2. Under these conditions, the two species primarily reacted via the fast SCR pathway in a 1:1 molar ratio, forming the unstable intermediate N2O3 52. This intermediate was then rapidly reduced by photogenerated electrons. This reaction pathway explains the absence of NO2 in the effluent. The presence of SO2 slightly inhibited the photocatalytic decomposition of NO (Fig. S16E, F). This inhibition can be attributed to SO2 acting as a scavenger for photogenerated holes, a mechanism previously documented in aqueous reaction systems53. The consumption of holes by SO2 disrupts the charge balance within the photocatalytic system, thereby altering the pathway for NO decomposition.

Charge carrier dynamics of modified CN-based catalysts
The prepared e-FCN photocatalyst successfully demonstrated an ability to reduce NO to N2 in the presence of 20% O2. This implies a capacity for the preferential adsorption and activation of NO over O2. To elucidate the key factors underlying this oxygen-tolerant NO reduction, we first investigated the charge carrier dynamics of e-CN, e-OCN, and e-FCN. UV-Vis diffuse reflectance spectra (UV-Vis DRS, Fig. S17A) revealed that: (1) e-FCN exhibits enhanced light absorption across both ultraviolet and visible regions compared with e-CN, a phenomenon attributed to F incorporation into the CN structure33; and (2) the absorption edge of e-OCN redshifts to the near-infrared region due to O modification35. To analyze charge carrier separation upon photoexcitation, we employed photoluminescence (PL) and time-resolved PL (TRPL) spectroscopy. The PL spectra (Fig. S17B) showed a progressive redshift in the emission peaks from 455 nm (e-CN) to 461 nm (e-OCN) and 465 nm (e-FCN), with a concomitant decrease in peak intensity (e-CN > e-OCN > e-FCN). The TRPL results (Fig. S17B and Table S7) further indicated that the average emission lifetime of e-FCN (5.55 ns) is longer than those of e-CN (2.05 ns) and e-OCN (3.23 ns). The reduced PL intensity and prolonged emission lifetime collectively suggest that F incorporation enhances charge carrier separation. This conclusion is consistently supported by photocurrent and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) measurements, which showed that the e-FCN electrode exhibits a higher photocurrent density (Fig. S17C) and lower electrical resistance (Fig. S17D) than e-CN and e-OCN.

Furthermore, determining the energy levels of these catalysts is essential for assessing how F modification influences the photocatalytic reaction from a thermodynamic perspective. The bandgap values, derived from Tauc plots, are 2.52 eV for e-CN, 2.05 eV for e-OCN, and 2.46 eV for e-FCN (Fig. S18A). The valence band (VB) edge positions, approximated from XPS VB spectra (Fig. S18B) according to the literature39, are +1.83 V RHE for e-CN, +1.52 V RHE for e-OCN, and +1.74 V RHE for e-FCN. Mott-Schottky plots measured at 1000 Hz (Fig. S18C) exhibit positive slopes, confirming n-type semiconductor behavior for all catalysts. The flat band potentials (Efb) are determined to be −0.69 V RHE for e-CN, −0.53 V RHE for e-OCN, and −0.72 V RHE for e-FCN; these values correspond to the conduction band (CB) edge levels54. An energy level diagram constructed from these findings is presented in Fig. S18D. The more negative CB edge of e-FCN (−0.72 V RHE), compared with e-CN (−0.69 V RHE) and e-OCN (−0.53 V RHE), indicates that e-FCN possesses a stronger driving force for the reduction of NO/NO2 to N2 [standard reduction potentials: E(NO/N2)=1.68 V RHE 55 and E(N2O/N2)=+1.77 V RHE 56]. However, thermodynamically, this more negative CB also provides a stronger driving force for the reduction of O2 to superoxide radical [•O2−, E(O2/•O2−)=-0.13 V RHE]57 or H2O2 [E(O2/H2O2)=0.68 V RHE]58. Thus, to resolve this thermodynamic conflict and identify the origin of the observed oxygen tolerance, subsequent investigations must focus on the charge carrier dynamics in NO/O2/Ar atmospheres.

To investigate the charge carrier dynamics of exfoliated CN-based catalysts under relevant conditions, microsecond transient absorption spectroscopy (μs-TAS) was employed, as its temporal resolution aligns with the timescales of the actual reaction kinetics. To distinguish the nature of the charge carriers, aqueous dispersions of e-CN were probed at 900 nm both with and without ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid dipotassium (EDTA). This well-established hole scavenger reveals the signature of long-lived electrons. As shown in Fig. S19A, the signal half-life (t50%) of e-CN was significantly prolonged from 35.5 μs to 63.6 μs upon the addition of EDTA. This observation confirms that the transient signal originates from photoinduced electrons, consistent with prior literature59.

Subsequently, the electron transfer kinetics of e-CN, e-OCN, and e-FCN were probed by introducing NO/O2/Ar atmospheres. Figures 5A, B and S19B demonstrated a decrease in the t50% values for all three catalysts under the NO or O2 atmosphere compared with the Ar atmosphere, confirming that electrons participate in activating both NO and O2 60. However, the catalysts exhibited distinct behavioral trends: e-CN showed similar reductions in t50% with NO or O2, indicating no significant specificity (Fig. S19B). On the other hand, e-OCN exhibited a larger reduction in t50% with O2 than NO (Fig. 5A), whereas e-FCN showed a substantial reduction with NO than O2 (Fig. 5B). These trends indicate that e-OCN preferentially facilitates the electron transfer to O2, whereas e-FCN favors the electron transfer to NO. To quantify this selectivity, the electron transfer efficiencies for O2 and NO, denoted as ETE(O2) and ETE(NO), were calculated from the t50% values according to an established literature method61. As listed in Table S8, e-FCN exhibited the highest ETE(NO) (30.2%) and the lowest ETE(O2) (6.2%), confirming its pronounced selectivity for activating NO over O2. This finding directly correlates with the observed catalytic performance, wherein e-FCN demonstrates an ability to reduce NO to N2 even in an oxygen-rich atmosphere.

In situ irradiation X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (ISI-XPS) was employed to probe light-induced binding energy shifts in exfoliated CN-based catalysts, thereby identifying functional groups active in photocatalysis62,63. Under illumination, the C 1s spectra exhibited a positive shift for C-M groups (where M=NHx, OH, F), indicating electron transfer from the C atoms to these functional groups (Figs. 5C and S20A, D). This interpretation was corroborated by a corresponding negative shift in the N 1s spectra of NHx groups, confirming their role as electron acceptors (Figs. 5D and S20B, E). In contrast, O 1s peaks associated with adsorbed H2O or CO2 exhibited no shift, indicating these species do not participate in the charge transfer process (Figs. 5E and S20C, F). Notably, in e-OCN, the C-OH peak in the O 1s spectrum exhibited a negative shift, identifying the OH group as an electron acceptor (Fig. S20F). An analogous negative shift was observed for the C–F group in the F 1s spectrum of e-FCN, indicating that F also acts as an electron acceptor (Fig. 5F). Collectively, these findings identify C-NHx, C-OH (in e-OCN), and C–F (in e-FCN) as direct participants in the photocatalytic reaction.

NO/O2 adsorption properties of modified CN-based catalysts
The above investigations into the charge carrier dynamics of CN-based catalysts have revealed significant variations in their electron transfer capabilities toward NO/O2. These findings warrant a further examination of the adsorption behavior and activation performance of NO/O2 on the CN-based catalyst surfaces. The nitrogen adsorption-desorption isotherms and pore-size distribution profiles of e-CN, e-OCN, and e-FCN are presented in Fig. S21. All three catalysts exhibit type II isotherms with an H3 hysteresis loop64. As summarized in Table S9, the Brunauer–Emmett–Teller (BET) surface area and pore volume increase in the order: e-CN < e-OCN < e-FCN. The preceding AFM and DLS analyses confirmed the successful exfoliation of the CN-based catalysts (Figs. S2 and 3). The introduction of electronegative O and F atoms effectively weakened the interlayer π-π interactions, thereby facilitating exfoliation. Owing to its higher electronegativity, F exerted a more pronounced effect, as evidenced by the decreasing order of both average particle thickness and average hydrodynamic particle size: e-CN > e-OCN > e-FCN. For layered materials, the specific surface area is primarily governed by the exposed surfaces of the exfoliated nanosheets. Theoretically, greater exfoliation reduces both the average number of layers and the overall thickness, resulting in a larger specific surface area36. The observed BET surface area and pore volume trend align well with this principle.

To evaluate the influence of exfoliation on photocatalytic NO decomposition activity, bulk CN-based photocatalysts were also prepared and tested as control samples under the identical reaction conditions. As illustrated in Fig. S22A–D, the photocatalytic NO removal efficiency and N2 selectivity of the bulk catalysts were significantly lower than those of the exfoliated catalysts in both Ar and 20% O2. The surface area and pore volume of the bulk catalysts are substantially smaller than those of the exfoliated catalysts (Fig. S21A, B and Table S9). This suggests that exfoliation increases the number of active sites exposed on the catalyst surface, thereby enhancing NO adsorption and subsequent activation36.

The NO and O2 adsorption capacities of e-CN, e-OCN, and e-FCN were evaluated using the NO/O2 temperature-programmed desorption (NO/O2-TPD) technique (Fig. 6A). To account for variations in specific surface area among the exfoliated catalysts, the TPD peak areas were normalized by the corresponding BET surface area, enabling a direct comparison of their intrinsic adsorption capacities. In the case of NO-TPD, e-FCN exhibited a higher desorption temperature and a larger normalized peak area than both e-CN and e-OCN, indicating a stronger and greater capacity for NO adsorption65. For O2-TPD, desorption events below 300°C were assigned to surface-adsorbed oxygen, while those between 300°C and 600°C were attributed to subsurface oxygen species66. In contrast to the NO adsorption results, e-FCN showed a significantly lower O2 desorption temperature and a smaller normalized peak area, suggesting a weaker and less extensive adsorption of O2 66. Conversely, e-OCN demonstrated the highest oxygen adsorption capacity of the three catalysts. The TPD peak areas were quantified by calibration with a standard gas mixture to establish the relationship between peak area and adsorbed gas concentration. As summarized in Table S10, this quantitative analysis confirms that e-FCN possesses the highest NO adsorption capacity (2.62 μmol·g−1) and the lowest O2 adsorption capacity (0.20 μmol·g−1), indicating a preferential adsorption of NO over O2. Collectively, the NO/O2-TPD results demonstrate that while e-CN and e-OCN exhibit comparable affinities for NO and O2, e-FCN remains largely inert towards O2.

To complement the NO/O2-TPD results, DFT calculations were conducted to analyze O2 and NO adsorption on the catalyst surfaces, despite the inherent challenge of modeling the exact catalyst under operational conditions. As shown in Fig. S23, the adsorption energies of O2 are more negative than those of NO for the optimized e-CN model [Eads(O2)=−0.18 eV, Eads(NO)=−0.09 eV] and the e-OCN model [Eads(O2)=−0.33 eV, Eads(NO)=-0.14 eV]. In contrast, for the e-FCN model [Eads(O2)=−0.08 eV, Eads(NO)=−0.21 eV], the adsorption energy of NO is significantly more negative than that of O2 (Fig. 6B, C). These theoretical results align with the experimental NO/O2-TPD data, confirming that e-FCN exhibits a strong preference for NO adsorption over O2, whereas e-CN and e-OCN show greater affinity for O2.

The above results have revealed that e-FCN preferentially adsorbs and activates NO, even in the presence of O2. However, the mechanism behind the inertness of e-FCN toward O2 adsorption, especially when compared with e-CN and e-OCN, requires further investigation. Previous studies have shown that the accumulation of the C=O bond, resulting from the oxidation of surface C atoms in CN catalysts, can be suppressed by surface fluorination that introduced the C–F bond, thereby mitigating C=O bond accumulation33. The formation of these C=O bonds on exfoliated CN-based catalysts was monitored using in situ Fourier-transform infrared (in situ FTIR) spectroscopy. Figure S24A–C showed that a newly generated band at 1725 cm−1 appeared upon exposure of e-CN, e-OCN, and e-FCN to 425 nm light irradiation, this band is consistent with the formation of a surface C=O bond. To verify this assignment, the in situ FTIR characterization was also carried out using 18O2 instead of O2. As shown in Fig. 7A–C, an analogous redshift to 1684 cm−1 occurred. The ratio of the wavenumbers, ν(C=18O)/ν(C=O), is close to the theoretical value of [μ(C=O)/μ(C=18O)]1/2=0.98, where μ(C=O)=6.86 and μ(C=18O)=7.20 represent the reduced masses of the respective C=O bonds67. Meanwhile, the FTIR bands associated with N-heterocyclic frameworks in the exfoliated catalysts and the C–F bond in e-FCN remained unchanged. These isotopic in situ FTIR results confirm the assignment of the 1725 cm−1 band to the C=O bond.

The exposure of both e-CN and e-OCN to O2/18O2 under 425 nm irradiation led to an increase in the band intensity corresponding to the C=18O/C=O bond (see Figs. 7A, B and S24A, B). On the other hand, the formation of the C=18O/C=O bond on e-FCN was significantly inhibited compared with that on e-CN and e-OCN. The spectral features of e-FCN remained consistent with those of N-heterocycles and the C–F bond (Figs. 7C and S24C). The time profiles of C=18O/C=O bond formation on e-CN, e-OCN, and e-FCN under irradiation in comparison with their dark control counterpart clearly show such spectral behavior (Figs. 7D and S24D). Collectively, these findings indicate that e-CN and e-OCN adsorb and activate O2 via light-driven C=O bond formation. The presence of C–F bonds in e-FCN inhibit this process. Consequently, e-FCN exhibits inert activity toward O2 activation but selectively adsorbs and activates NO for reduction under light irradiation, even in the presence of excess O2.

In situ monitoring of NO photoreaction over modified CN-based catalysts
The NO/O2 adsorption results demonstrate that the presence of the C–F bond in CN suppresses the formation of the C=O bond, rendering e-FCN inert towards O2. To investigate the NO photoconversion process in the presence of O2, in situ FTIR spectroscopy was employed to monitor the chemical transformation process. The FTIR spectra of initial NO adsorption on e-CN, e-OCN, and e-FCN reveal distinct bands (Fig. S25): one at 1690–1694 cm−1, corresponding to adsorbed (NO)2 species on the surface68, and others at 1273 and 1411–1413 cm−1, indicative of bridged (NO)2 species17. These bands (1273, 1411-1413, and 1694 cm−1) increase gradually over time (Fig. S25A, C, E), and e-FCN consistently exhibits higher band intensities compared with e-CN and e-OCN, thereby confirming stronger NO binding on e-FCN (Fig. S25B, D, F). The signals at 1273 and 1411–1413 cm−1 are typically attributed to the symmetric vibration of bridging bidentate NO3−69. The conventional assignment of the 1273 and 1411–1413 cm−1 bands to symmetric vibrations of bridging bidentate NO3− is inconsistent with the absence of asymmetric vibrational modes in the 1500–1700 cm−1 region. An alternative interpretation, which aligns with the observed spectral features, is that these bands originate from a bridged (NO)2 dimer adsorbed on the catalyst.

The assignment of the observed feature to an (NO)2 dimer was confirmed unequivocally using 15NO isotope-substituted in situ FTIR spectroscopy. As shown in Fig. S26, the spectrum exhibited a corresponding redshift to lower wavenumber. The experimental ν(15N)/ν(N) ratios showed close agreement with theoretical values predicted for an (NO)2 dimer (Table S11), thereby confirming this assignment70. While complementary DFT calculations were employed to investigate NO adsorption behavior and interactions between co-adsorbed NO molecules on the e-FCN surface, it is important to note the inherent difficulty in modeling the precise catalyst structure under realistic catalytic conditions. One or two NO molecules were introduced onto the e-FCN surface slab (Fig. 6C–F). Computed adsorption energies revealed a more stable configuration for the (NONO) dimer, with a total Eads(NONO) of -0.31 eV for the dimer system, compared with Eads(NO)=-0.21 eV for a single NO molecule (Fig. 6C, D). This enhanced stability arises from both π back-donation to the NO ligands and direct attractive interactions between the co-adsorbed NO molecules. Charge density analysis indicated significant electron accumulation at the adsorption sites, increasing from 0.36 |e| for a single NO molecule to 0.69 |e| for the dimer system (Fig. 6E, F), consistent with enhanced electron transfer from the e-FCN substrate. The total charge associated with the dimer was less than the sum of the two isolated NO adsorbates. This charge redistribution, combined with the adjacent geometry of the two N atoms, suggests a mechanism that mitigates inter-adsorbate repulsion and facilitates N–N coupling. The assignment of vibrational bands to an (NO)2 dimer, confirmed through in situ isotopic FTIR and theoretical calculations, indicates that N–N bond formation occurs via a partial overlap of electron density between adjacent N atoms25.

Upon irradiating NO adsorbed on the catalysts, a new band appears at 2314 cm−1, indicating the presence of adsorbed N2O on the catalyst surface, as shown in Fig. S27A, C, E71,72. Initially, this band increases with irradiation time for e-CN, e-OCN, and e-FCN, suggesting the formation of N2O as an intermediate in the decomposition of NO. However, after 18 min, the band begins to decrease on e-FCN (Fig. S27F), while it continues to rise on e-CN and e-OCN (Fig. S27B, D). This contrasting behavior between the catalysts suggests that the N2O intermediates undergo further transformation on e-FCN but accumulate on e-CN and e-OCN. This observation is consistent with the finding that N2O production during the photocatalytic NO conversion was minimal on e-FCN but significant on e-CN and e-OCN (see Fig. 2A). These results highlight the critical role of e-FCN in promoting the photocatalytic reduction of N2O intermediates to N2. Notably, a band at 1555 cm−1 was observed for all catalysts under light irradiation (Fig. S27A, C, E), indicating the accumulation of bidentate NO3− on the catalyst surface73. Among the catalysts, e-OCN exhibits the highest NO3− accumulation. This finding is consistent with the observation that NO3− selectivity for e-OCN is higher than that for e-CN and e-FCN (see above Fig. 2A). Definitive confirmation of the N2O and NO3− feature assignments was achieved using 15NO isotope-substituted in situ FTIR spectroscopy. The spectrum showed a corresponding redshift (Fig. 8), and the experimental ν(15N)/ν(N) ratios closely matched theoretical values for an N2O and NO3− (Table S11), validating the assignment70. The band area changes of 15N2O and 15NO3− were also consistent with those of N2O and NO3−. Consequently, it is revealed that NO photoconversion in O2 proceeds predominantly via an oxidative pathway on e-CN/e-OCN but shifts to a reductive pathway on e-FCN.

The role of direct electron transfer in photocatalytic NO decomposition can be evaluated by introducing potassium dichromate (K2Cr2O7) as an electron scavenger. Figure 9A shows that the addition of K2Cr2O7 significantly decreases NO removal and N2 selectivity for e-FCN under 425 nm light irradiation in 20% O2. This finding underscores the critical importance of electron transfer in NO conversion. Moreover, the production of NO2 during photocatalytic NO decomposition over e-FCN increases markedly in the presence of K2Cr2O7, suggesting that photoinduced holes, enhanced by electron scavenging, primarily drive the oxidation of NO to NO2 in the e-FCN/Cr system74. Conversely, the use of EDTA as a hole scavenger only moderately reduces NO removal and slightly decreases N2 selectivity under the identical reaction conditions (Fig. 9B). Similar trends are observed for e-OCN, as shown in Fig. S28, where the effects of K2Cr2O7 and EDTA are consistent with those observed for e-FCN. These results confirm that electron transfer, rather than hole transfer, plays the dominant role in the photocatalytic NO decomposition on both e-FCN and e-OCN.

The effect of hole scavenging on the reaction pathway was also investigated by carrying out the isotopic labeling experiments for the e-FCN/5EDTA catalyst. First, an experiment was performed with a 4% 15NO gas mixture in 20% O2/Ar. Pre-reaction GC-MS analysis (Fig. S29A) confirmed the absence of N2 contamination, with only a characteristic O2 peak detected. Following a 2-h photocatalytic reaction, GC-MS analysis revealed that the evolved N2 originated exclusively from the decomposition of 15NO, as indicated by the sole presence of 15N2 (Fig. S29B). This result demonstrates that scavenging photoinduced holes had no appreciable effect on N2 formation. Subsequently, an experiment was conducted with a 4% NO gas mixture in 20% 18O2/Ar. Pre-reaction analysis (Fig. S29C) confirmed the exclusive presence of 18O2, ruling out significant atmospheric O2 contamination. The post-reaction mass spectrum of O2 (Fig. S29D) displayed signals only for 18O2, indicating that no new O2 was generated through the hole-induced decomposition of EDTA. A parallel experiment conducted with EDTA in Ar corroborated these findings, showing a moderate reduction in NO removal and a slight decrease in N2 selectivity (Fig. S29E, F). Furthermore, hole scavenging inhibited O2 formation (Fig. 9C). Collectively, these results indicate that in the presence of EDTA, NO is converted to N2 through a photoreduction process without concomitant O2 generation.

To elucidate the pathway for the photocatalytic conversion of NO to O2, EPR spectra of e-FCN and e-FCN/5EDTA were compared before and after the reaction. As shown in Fig. S30A, the EPR signal intensity for the used e-FCN/5EDTA catalyst, measured at 273 K, was significantly higher than that of its pristine state, whereas the signal for e-FCN remained largely unchanged. For enhanced spectral resolution, EPR measurements were conducted at 77 K. At this temperature, the EPR spectrum of the used e-FCN/5EDTA exhibited an additional hyperfine structure with g-values of 2.002 and 1.995, along with an intensified signal at g=2.007 (Fig. 9D). These emergent signals are assigned to O3− species75. This observation effectively precludes the involvement of •O2−. This species is notoriously difficult to detect by direct EPR due to its rapid relaxation time and broad spectral features76, which contrast sharply with the well-defined hyperfine structure observed here. It is proposed that O3− forms via the reaction of O− with molecular O2 at 77 K, facilitated by weak covalent bonding between the π-electrons of O2 and the free electron on O−77. This adduct is unstable at elevated temperatures; heating above 150 K causes the dissociation of the weak bond, leading to the disappearance of O3− and the regeneration of O−78. This mechanism accounts for the intensified EPR signal at g=2.005 for the used e-FCN/5EDTA measured at 273 K: The signal for O− typically occurs at g=2.00579, which coincides with the intrinsic signal from unpaired electrons in CN-based catalysts. The accumulation of O− species thus enhances the overall signal intensity at this position. Conversely, the EPR spectrum of e-FCN at 77 K showed minimal change after the reaction (Fig. 9D). The EDTA scavenging tests and EPR results collectively reveal the NO conversion mechanism: NO is reduced by electrons to N2 and O−, which is then oxidized by holes to form O2. Scavenging holes with EDTA inhibit the final oxidation step, causing O− accumulation on e-FCN/5EDTA and preventing O2 formation, which was not observed on e-FCN.

The results of K2Cr2O7 scavenger tests indicate that the photoinduced holes in e-FCN and e-OCN oxidize NO to NO2 only in the presence of O2 (Figs. 9A and S28A, B). Notably, Fig. 2A demonstrates the formation of NO3− during the photocatalytic conversion of NO over e-FCN and e-OCN, suggesting that specific reactive oxygen species, such as •OH, 1O2, and •O2−, facilitate the oxidation of NO to NO3−22. Comparative analyses employing various scavengers, including tert-butanol (TBA) for •OH (Fig. S31), L-histidine (His) for 1O2 (Fig. S32), and L-ascorbic acid (AA) for •O2− (Fig. S33), were conducted. Figures S31 and 32 indicate that the introduction of TBA and His does not significantly affect NO removal efficiency or N2 selectivity, implying minimal contributions from •OH and 1O2 in the photocatalytic NO decomposition over e-FCN and e-OCN. In contrast, the use of AA as a •O2− scavenger moderately impairs NO removal, promotes NO2 formation, and suppresses NO3− production in the case of e-OCN (Fig. S33A, B). A similar trend is observed for e-FCN, where AA moderately reduces NO removal, increases N2 selectivity, and decreases NO3− formation (Fig. S33C, D). These findings indicate that •O2− selectively reacts with NO to produce NO3−14. Moreover, EPR spin-trapping experiments using 5,5-dimethyl-1-pyrroline-N-oxide (DMPO) to capture •O2− reveal that the amount of •O2− generated follows the order: e-OCN > e-CN > e-FCN (Fig. S30B). This trend aligns with catalytic performance (Fig. 2A) and in situ FTIR results (Figs. 8 and S27), which show a similar decreasing order for NO3− formation. Together, these results confirm that •O2− is the key species responsible for NO3− production during the photocatalytic conversion of NO over these catalysts.

The scavenger tests and EPR analysis results provide valuable insights into the mechanisms underlying photocatalytic NO decomposition. Initially, electron transfer plays a pivotal role in converting NO primarily into N2. Additionally, the following hole transfer facilitates the oxidation of O− species to O2, further contributing to NO decomposition. Moreover, O2 undergoes activation to form •O2−, which subsequently oxidizes NO to NO3−. Among the tested catalysts, e-FCN is almost inert towards O2, resulting in the lowest activity for O2 activation to •O2−. Consequently, e-FCN achieves the highest N2 selectivity and the lowest NO3− selectivity for NO decomposition.

Based on the above results, the photocatalytic reaction mechanism of NO conversion on e-FCN is proposed and illustrated in Fig. 10A. The ISI-XPS (Figs. 5C–F and S20) results identify C-NHx, C-OH (in e-OCN), and C–F (in e-FCN) as direct participants in the photocatalytic reaction. The NO/O2-TPD (Fig. 6A), theoretical calculations (Fig. 6B, C), and in situ FTIR for O2 photoactivation (Figs. 7 and S24) results indicate that e-FCN preferentially adsorbs NO in the presence of O2. The strongly electron-withdrawing F atom is bonded to the CN framework via C–F bonds, polarizing the adjacent π-ring and thereby enhancing its interaction with the NO molecule through the N atom12,80. The in situ FTIR (Figs. S25 and 26) and theoretical calculation (Fig. 6D–F) results from NO dark adsorption on e-FCN reveal a band corresponding to (NO)2, indicating that e-FCN forms (NO)2 on its surface after adsorbing two NO molecules, thereby promoting N-N coupling. The in situ FTIR results from NO photoreaction (Figs. 8 and S27) on e-FCN reveal that the (NO)2 band area is significantly reduced from that of NO dark adsorption, accompanied by the appearance of N2O intermediate. This suggests that (NO)2 adsorbed on the surface of e-FCN undergoes N–N coupling, forming N2O as an intermediate. Furthermore, these in situ FTIR results show that the N2O band area initially increases and then decreases over time, indicating that N2O intermediates on the e-FCN surface are further reduced to N2 by photo-induced electrons.

As shown in Figs. 9B, C and S29D, scavenging holes in e-FCN leads to a slight decrease in the NO removal rate and N2 selectivity, but completely inhibits O2 production. This confirms that the evolution of O2 during the photocatalytic decomposition of NO is driven by hole oxidation. Under irradiation, e-FCN should generate both electrons and holes, and the following interface charge transfer occurs simultaneously to maintain overall charge balance in the photocatalyst. However, the transfer of photoinduced electrons and holes occurs at different timescales due to differences in charge transfer kinetics25. After photoinduced electrons reduce (NO)2 to N2, N2 easily desorbs from the surface of e-FCN, leaving behind two O− species. These species are then oxidized by the photoinduced holes to produce O2, regenerating catalytic sites.

The photocatalytic results in Fig. 2A demonstrate that NO is oxidized to NO3− over e-OCN/e-CN, confirming that NO oxidation is the dominant reaction on the e-OCN/e-CN surface. EPR analysis of •O2− (Fig. S30B), along with •O2− scavenger experiments on e-OCN (Fig. S33A, B), revealed that •O2− is the primary active species responsible for oxidizing NO to NO3−. Notably, photoinduced electron scavenger experiments on e-OCN (Fig. S28A, B) led to a significant reduction in NO3− formation, accompanied by the generation of NO2 and an increase in its proportion. This suggests that photoinduced holes in e-OCN oxidize NO to NO2. The •O2− scavenger experiments yielded similar results, further supporting the role of photoinduced holes in oxidizing NO to NO2. Based on these findings, we propose a reaction mechanism for NO conversion on e-OCN and e-CN (Fig. 10B). NO primarily undergoes oxidation, where photoinduced holes facilitate its conversion to NO2, while O2 is reduced to •O2− by photoinduced electrons. Finally, •O2− oxidizes NO/NO2 to NO3−.
