## Methods

Chemicals
The chemicals used in this work include the following. Melamine, glycolic acid, ammonium bromide (NH4Br), ammonium fluoride (NH4F), titanium(III) chloride solution (10-15 wt% TiCl3), Pluronic F127 (C3H6O·C2H4O)x, bismuth(III) nitrate pentahydrate [Bi(NO3)3·5H2O], EDTA salt dihydrate, potassium dichromate (K2Cr2O7), L-ascorbic acid (AA), tert-butanol (TBA), L-histidine (His), DMPO, and ethanol were obtained from Merck Corporation. NO standard gas (500 ppmv NO, Ar balance), ultra-high purity Ar (99.999%), O2 standard gas (20 vol% O2, Ar balance), CO2 standard gas (5 vol% CO2, Ar balance), NO2 standard gas (500 ppmv NO2, Ar balance), and SO2 standard gas (500 ppmv SO2, Ar balance) were purchased from Deokyang Company. For isotopic labeling experiments, 15N-labeled sodium nitrite (Na15NO2) and 18O-labeled molecular oxygen (18O2) were obtained from Merck Corporation. 15NO was synthesized according to the reaction shown in Eq. 1, following a reported procedure81. The resulting 15NO gas was collected in a gas sample bag and subsequently introduced into the reactor using a mini gas pump. All chemicals used were of analytical grade and were used as received without further purification. Ultrapure deionized water (18 MΩ·cm) was produced using a Millipore system.

3Na15NO2 + H2SO4 → 215NO + Na15NO3 + Na2SO4 + H2O (1)

Catalyst preparation
Preparation of bulk-CN and thermally exfoliated CN (e-CN). The bulk-CN was prepared through the thermal decomposition of melamine (8.00 g, 63.43 mmol)37. Melamine was heated in a lidded crucible at 550°C for 3 h under static air, with a controlled heating rate of 5°C·min−1. The resulting product was collected and ground into a fine powder for subsequent applications.

The e-CN was prepared via a modified thermal exfoliation method36. In this process, 1.0 g of the prepared bulk-CN was heated in a lidded crucible at 500°C for 2 h under static air, with a heating rate maintained at 5°C·min−1. The final product was collected and ground into a fine powder for further use.

Preparation of bulk oxygen-modified CN (bulk-OCN) and thermally exfoliated oxygen-modified CN (e-OCN). The preparation of bulk-OCN was achieved by directly incorporating glycolic acid into the conventional condensation process35. Initially, melamine (8.00 g, 63.43 mmol) and glycolic acid (0.72 g, 9.52 mmol) were combined and homogenized through grinding. The mixture was then placed in a covered crucible and subjected to heating at 550°C for 3 h under static air conditions, with a controlled heating rate of 5°C·min−1. After the heating process, the crucible was allowed to cool naturally to room temperature. The resulting solid was then dispersed in water to remove any unreacted substances, stirred overnight, centrifuged, thoroughly washed with deionized water, and dried for further applications.

The e-OCN was prepared using the modified thermal exfoliation method based on the aforementioned procedure36. Specifically, 1.0 g of the prepared bulk-OCN was heated in a lidded crucible at 500°C for 2 h under static air, maintaining a heating rate of 5°C·min−1. The product obtained from this process was finely ground into powder for further use.

Preparation of bulk fluoride-modified CN (bulk-FCN) and thermally exfoliated fluoride-modified CN (e-FCN). The bulk-FCN was prepared through the direct addition of NH4F into the conventional condensation process34. Specifically, melamine (8.00 g, 63.43 mmol) and NH4F (1.06 g, 28.54 mmol) were combined and homogenized via grinding. The resulting mixture was transferred to a covered crucible and heated at 550°C for 3 h under static air conditions, with a controlled heating rate of 5°C·min−1. After cooling naturally to room temperature, the solid was dispersed in water to remove unreacted substances, stirred overnight, centrifuged, washed with deionized water, and then dried for further applications.

The e-FCN was prepared using a modified thermal exfoliation method based on the above procedure36. In this process, 1.0 g of the prepared bulk-FCN was heated in a covered crucible at 500°C for 2 h under static air conditions, maintaining a heating rate of 5°C·min−1. The resulting material was collected, finely powdered, and stored for further use.

The C and N content was determined using elemental analysis. A measured quantity of the catalyst was digested with concentrated HNO3 as an oxidant, and the F content in the resulting solution was quantified via ion chromatography. This measurement was then used to calculate the F content in the original catalyst. Based on this method, the atomic ratio of F/C was determined. Accordingly, the catalyst is denoted as e-F(X)CN, where X represents the atomic percentage (at%) of F relative to C.

For comparative analysis, four additional e-FCN catalysts were synthesized by varying the initial NH4F amount. These were labeled as e-F(0.05)CN, e-F(0.15)CN, e-F(0.20)CN, and e-F(0.25)CN, corresponding to initial NH4F amounts of 0.53 g (14.27 mmol), 1.59 g (42.81 mmol), 2.12 g (57.08 mmol), and 2.65 g (71.35 mmol), respectively. Unless otherwise stated, e-FCN in this study refers to e-F(0.10)CN.

Preparation of mesoporous TiO2-x (mp-TiO2-x). The mp-TiO2-x was prepared using a modified Ti3+ self-doping method25. A light-yellow, mesoporous TiO2-x powder was synthesized via a modified Ti3+ self-doping methodology. The process began with the dissolution of Pluronic F127 (0.25 g, 0.02 mmol) in ethanol (1.00 mL). An aqueous TiCl3 solution (2.60 mL, 4.00 mmol) was then combined with the ethanolic surfactant solution. Following solvent removal through heated stirring, the resultant gel was transferred to a crucible and subjected to thermal treatment. This calcination step involved a temperature ramp of 5°C·min−1 to a final temperature of 600°C, which was held for 3 h. The target mp-TiO2-x compound was obtained as a light-yellow solid after cooling to room temperature.

Preparation of F-doped mp-TiO2-x (F-mp-TiO2-x). The F-mp-TiO2-x was synthesized via an impregnation method48. First, a 0.1 M NH4F solution was prepared by dissolving 0.37 g (0.01 mol) of NH4F in 100 mL of deionized water. Next, 0.3 mL of this solution was diluted with 29.7 mL of deionized water to obtain 30 mL of a 1 mM NH4F solution. Subsequently, 1 g of mp-TiO2-x was dispersed in the diluted NH4F solution under continuous stirring. The mixture was then heated until complete solvent evaporation, yielding the final F-doped product, F-mp-TiO2-x. The F doping concentration in F-mp-TiO2-x matched that of the e-F(0.10)CN.

Preparation of BiOBr and BiOF. The BiOBr and BiOF were synthesized using a modified method based on previously reported literature49. For the preparation of BiOBr, NH4Br (0.98 g, 0.01 mol) was dissolved in 25 mL of deionized water to form an NH4Br solution. Simultaneously, Bi(NO3)3·5H2O (4.85 g, 0.01 mol) was dissolved in 25 mL of deionized water to prepare a Bi(NO3)3 solution. The NH4Br solution was then added dropwise into the Bi(NO3)3 solution. The resulting suspension was stirred for 18 h, followed by centrifugation. The precipitate was washed repeatedly with deionized water, dried, and collected as BiOBr. The same procedure was followed for the synthesis of BiOF, with NH4F (0.37 g, 0.01 mol) replacing NH4Br as the precursor.

Photocatalytic NO decomposition evaluation. As shown in Fig. S36, the NO decomposition photoreaction was performed using a 300 mL glass reactor with a closed circulation system25. For testing, a quartz plate containing a 2 cm × 2 cm groove was used to support a uniform dispersion of 0.15 g of catalyst. This plate was then placed inside the reactor, which allowed for light irradiation via a 3 cm-diameter quartz window. Various LED light sources (365, 385, 405, 425, 445, and 465 nm) were employed, and the light intensities reaching the catalyst were measured at 18, 23, 32, 50, 50, and 50 mW·cm−2, respectively, using a Newport 1918-R power meter. The catalyst surface temperature was monitored using a thermocouple. To examine the influence of temperature on catalytic performance, the reactor was externally heated using heating tape, enabling precise temperature control. A continuous gas flow containing 2.0 ppmv NO and varying concentrations (0, 5, 10, 15, and 20 vol%) of O2 was introduced into the glass reactor at different flow rates (10, 20, 30, and 40 mL·min−1). Ar was used as the balance gas in the reaction mixture. The RH of the gas stream was controlled by passing Ar gas through a stainless-steel water bottle. To evaluate the impact of coexisting gases (CO2, NO2, and SO2) on catalytic performance, varying concentrations of each gas were individually introduced into the reactor. The photocatalytic NO decomposition process was initiated by LED light irradiation after achieving the NO adsorption equilibrium.

The NOx levels were determined using a NOx analyzer (Thermo Scientific 17i), while gas chromatography-mass spectrometry (GC-MS, Agilent 7890A-5975B) was employed for the analysis of N2O, N2, and O2. After the reaction, the catalyst was suspended in water and agitated for 1 h to dissolve any absorbed nitrogen-containing compounds. The resulting mixture was filtered, and the filtrate was injected into an ion chromatograph (Thermo Scientific Dionex ICS-900) to quantify the NO3− concentration in the solution. To assess the accumulation of NO3− on the catalyst surface over 12 consecutive cycles, 12 parallel experiments were conducted, each subjected to 1-12 reaction cycles. Upon completion, the NO3− content adsorbed on the catalyst surface was quantified. NO removal efficiency and N2 selectivity were calculated based on inlet and outlet concentrations of reactants and products using Eqs. 2 and 3, respectively.

NO removal = ([NO]in - [NO]out) / [NO]in × 100% (2)

N2 selectivity = 2[N2]out / (2[N2]out + 2[N2O]out + [NO2]out) × 100% (3)

Isotopic labeling experiments. Isotopic labeling experiments were conducted in a sealed reactor. A 0.15 g catalyst sample was evenly dispersed into a 2 cm × 2 cm groove on a quartz glass plate. Prior to the photoreaction, the reactor was subjected to repeated evacuation and purging cycles. To identify the nitrogen source in N2 formation, the reactor was charged with a gas mixture of 4 vol% 15NO, 20% O2, and Ar (balance) at ambient pressure. Photocatalytic NO decomposition was then initiated under irradiation from a 425 nm LED light source. After a 2-h reaction, the gaseous products were analyzed by GC-MS using an HP-PLOT Molesieve 5A column (30 m × 0.32 mm × 15 μm) for the detection of 15N2 and O2. To determine the origin of the newly generated O2, a separate experiment was performed using a gas mixture of 4 vol% NO, 20% 18O2, and Ar (balance). Following an identical 2-h photoreaction, the product gases were analyzed by GC-MS to quantify N2, O2, and 18O2.

Characterizations. The study involves a comprehensive characterization of catalysts employing a variety of analytical techniques. XRD patterns were obtained using an XPERT-PRO X-ray diffractometer equipped with CuKα radiation. AFM imaging was performed using an NT-MDT Solver Next atomic force microscope. Particle size distribution was determined by DLS using an Omni zeta potential analyzer (Brookhaven Instruments Corporation, USA). Elemental analysis of C and N was conducted using an EA ICE-440 elemental analyzer.

XPS measurements were performed with a Thermo Scientific XPS K-alpha instrument, utilizing non-monochromatic Al-Kα radiation (with an electron work function Φ=3.90 eV). The VB edge positions were estimated from the XPS VB spectra using Eq. 4. ISI-XPS was performed using the ESCALAB 250Xi XPS system. During the characterization, a 425 nm LED light source was positioned approximately 20 cm from the prepared samples to examine light-induced changes in electron density on the catalyst surfaces. Deconvolution and peak fitting for C 1s, N 1s, O 1s, and F 1s were carried out using XPSPEAK software39.

E(RHE) = Φ + E(eV) - 4.44 (4)

[E(RHE) is the potential vs RHE at pH 7; E(eV) is the VB level from the XPS result; Φ=3.90 (the work function of the XPS equipment)].

EPR spectra were acquired using a JEOL JES-FA200 spectrometer under specific conditions: microwave power at 0.93 mW, frequency of 9.65 GHz, modulation amplitude of 10 G, and a time constant of 20.48 ms. The superoxide radical (•O2−) was detected using the radical spin-trapping reagent DMPO. The typical testing temperature for catalyst and •O2− analysis was 298 K; however, detecting the O3− signal required measurements at 77 K75,77,78. Solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy of 13C, 1H, and 19F (solid-state 13C, 1H, and 19F NMR) was performed on a Bruker Avance III 500WB spectrometer. Diffuse reflectance UV-visible absorption spectroscopy (UV-DRS) was conducted using a Shimadzu UV-2401PC spectrophotometer. The bandgap was determined from the Tauc plot using Eq. 5.

[F(R) × hν]2 = A × (hν - Eg) (5)

(h is Planck’s constant; ν is photon frequency; A is a constant; Eg is the bandgap).

Steady-state and time-resolved PL spectra were obtained using a Horiba FluoroMax-4 spectrophotometer with an excitation wavelength of 425 nm. Microsecond transient absorption spectroscopy (μs-TAS) was conducted in transmission mode using a nanosecond Nd:YAG laser (Spectra-Physics, LAB-130-10) as the pump source. The 355 nm laser output was focused onto the sample films with an excitation density of 0.5 mJ·cm−2 and a repetition rate of 10 Hz. A 100 W tungsten-halogen lamp (ASBN-W) generated the probe beam at 900 nm, with long-pass and short-pass filters placed between the lamp and the sample to minimize short-wavelength radiation and sample heating. The resulting absorption changes were directed into a monochromator (Spectral Products, CM110) for wavelength selection. A silicon photodiode detected the time-resolved signal, which was amplified by a broadband preamplifier and recorded using an oscilloscope (Tektronix DPO4012). Transient decay profiles averaged over 256 laser pulses to improve the signal-to-noise ratio. For in situ μs-TAS experiments, measurements were performed under simulated reaction conditions, with the sample films exposed to a controlled gas environment. Prior to testing, the cell was purged for 30 min with either Ar, O2, or a 500 ppmv NO/Ar mixture to ensure equilibrium adsorption of reactant molecules on the film surface. This approach enabled in situ μs-TAS studies under varying atmospheric conditions.

The N2 adsorption-desorption isotherms were obtained at 77 K, employing a Quantachrome NOVA 2200e instrument. Temperature-programmed desorption of NO or O2 (NO/O2-TPD) was performed using an AutoChem 2920 Chemisorption analyzer. The quantitative relationship between the TPD signal peak area and the adsorbed NO/O2 concentration was calibrated using an NO/O2 standard gas mixture, establishing a standard curve. This calibration was then applied to determine the NO/O2 adsorption capacity on the catalyst surface.

In situ Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (in situ FTIR) was employed to track the formation of reaction intermediates during the photocatalytic decomposition of NO. The measurements were conducted using a PerkinElmer IR spectrometer equipped with a diffuse-reflectance cell featuring a ZnSe window. O2 was adsorbed on the catalyst in the cell that was pretreated at 150°C under an Ar gas flow for 30 min. After cooling, a continuous flow of 500 ppmv NO and 20 vol% O2/Ar was introduced and maintained constant throughout the dark adsorption process and the following photoreaction under 425 nm light irradiation. According to the reported literature33, in situ FTIR spectroscopy was employed to monitor the formation of C=O bonds on CN-based catalysts. This was achieved by exposing the catalysts to O2 both in the dark and under 425 nm light irradiation.

To verify the FTIR peak assignments, isotopic labeling was performed using 15NO as the reaction gas. Upon substitution of N with 15N, all observed peaks shifted to lower wavenumbers, consistent with the expected isotopic effect67,70. Similarly, when monitoring C=O bond formation using 18O2 in place of O2, an analogous shift to lower wavenumbers was observed. The relationship between the vibrational frequency (ν), the reduced mass (μ), and the bond force constant (k) is given by Eq. 6. In most cases (e.g., C=O, NO dimer, and NO3−), the reduced mass (μ) can be calculated using Eq. 7, which is based on a diatomic vibrational model. However, for N2O, the calculation must follow Eq. 8 due to its triatomic vibrational model.

ν = 1 / (2π) * sqrt(k / μ) (6)

μ = (m1 × m2) / (m1 + m2) (7)

μ(N2O) = mN × (mN + 2mO) / (2 * (mN + mO)) (8)

Photoelectrochemical (PEC) measurements. PEC experiments were conducted using a GAMRY Interface 1010 electrochemical workstation with a three-electrode setup. The reference electrode was Ag/AgCl, and the counter electrode was a platinum sheet (1 cm × 1 cm). The working electrode was prepared by immobilizing the catalyst onto a plate of indium-doped tin oxide (ITO) conductive glass (1 cm × 1 cm), using a casting technique. To prepare the working electrode, 6 mg of catalyst was dispersed in a solution of 540 μL ethanol and 60 μL of a 5.0 wt% Nafion ethanolic solution. After sonication for 30 min, 100 μL of this suspension was applied to the pre-sonicated ITO electrode, ensuring a catalyst loading of 1 mg·cm−2. Once the solvent evaporated, the working electrode was ready for PEC testing.

The characterization of the photocurrent was conducted in a 0.1 M Na2SO4 solution at pH 7. Data were acquired at a bias of −0.5 V vs the reversible hydrogen electrode (VRHE) under chopped light irradiation at 425 nm, with alternating 30-s periods of light-on and light-off. EIS was performed by applying an AC voltage with a 5 mV amplitude across a frequency range from 105 Hz to 0.01 Hz, under dark open-circuit potential (OCP) conditions, in the same 0.1 M Na2SO4 solution at pH 7. The Mott-Schottky plots were measured in 0.1 M Na2SO4 solution at pH 7, using a fixed frequency of 1000 Hz in the dark. All recorded potentials were corrected for iR compensation and referenced to the RHE at pH 7, as specified by Eq. 9. It is important to note that a consistent set of photoelectrodes was used throughout all PEC measurements.

E(RHE) = E(Ag/AgCl) + 0.059 × pH + 0.197 (9)

AQYs for N2 formation. The quantum yields (AQYs) for N2 formation were determined at various wavelengths (365, 385, 405, 425, 445, and 465 nm) using Eq. 10.

AQY(%) = (niN2 × NA) / (EAλt / hc) (10)

In this equation, niN2 is the number of generated N2 molecules, i the number of electrons required for the reduction of NO to N2 (2NO+4e−→N2+2O2−, i=4), NA the Avogadro constant (6.02 × 1023), E the intensity of light (W·cm−2), A the area of light irradiation (A=4 cm2), λ the wavelength of the LED lamp, t the duration of illumination (t=1800 s), h the Planck constant (6.62 × 10−34 J·s), and c the speed of light (3.0 × 108 m·s−1).

Scavenging test for charge carriers. The scavenging agents employed for mechanistic investigation were EDTA, K2Cr2O7, L-ascorbic acid (AA), tert-butanol (TBA), and L-histidine (His), for scavenging hole (h+), electron (e−), •O2−, hydroxyl radical (•OH), and singlet oxygen (1O2), respectively82,83. To evaluate the hole scavenging effect, 0.15 g of e-FCN was dispersed in 10 mL aqueous solution of EDTA, followed by agitation and heating for water evaporation. Catalysts were denoted as e-FCN/1EDTA, e-FCN/3EDTA, and e-FCN/5EDTA, corresponding to EDTA concentrations of 1 mM, 3 mM, and 5 mM, with adsorbed EDTA acting as a hole scavenger. Similarly, employing analogous methods, catalysts were prepared using solutions of K2Cr2O7, AA, TBA, and His to scavenge e−, •O2−, •OH, and 1O2, resulting in e-FCN/1Cr, e-FCN/3Cr, e-FCN/5Cr (from 1 mM, 3 mM, and 5 mM K2Cr2O7); e-FCN/1AA, e-FCN/3AA, e-FCN/5AA (from 1 mM, 3 mM, and 5 mM AA); e-FCN/1TBA, e-FCN/3TBA, e-FCN/5TBA (from 1 mM, 3 mM, and 5 mM TBA); e-FCN/1His, e-FCN/3His, e-FCN/5His (from 1 mM, 3 mM, and 5 mM His). Subsequently, the prepared e-FCN/EDTA, e-FCN/Cr, e-FCN/AA, e-FCN/TBA, and e-FCN/His catalysts were assessed for photocatalytic NO decomposition. The e-OCN-based catalysts, including e-OCN/EDTA, e-OCN/Cr, e-OCN/AA, e-OCN/TBA, and e-OCN/His, were prepared using a similar procedure for testing photocatalytic NO decomposition.

Theoretical calculation methods. In this study, all calculations were conducted using a periodic slab model implemented in the Vienna Ab Initio Simulation Package (VASP)84–87 with the projected augmented wave (PAW) method88,89. Exchange-correlation effects were described within the generalized gradient approximation (GGA) using the Perdew–Burke–Ernzerhof (PBE) functional, and a plane-wave kinetic energy cutoff of 400 eV was applied. To minimize interactions between periodic images, a vacuum layer of 10 Å was introduced along the z-axis. Dispersion corrections were included via the DFT-D3 scheme90,91. The (F/O)CN catalyst models were constructed based on previously reported literature and subsequently optimized to eliminate any structurally unreasonable coordination geometries32,33,35,41. The atomic coordinates for all computational models used in this study are available in Supplementary Data 1. The adsorption energies (Eads) of NO and O2 were calculated as described in Eq. 11:

Eads = E*species - E* - Especies (11)

where E*species, E*, and Especies represent the total energies of the adsorbed system, the (F/O)CN substrate, and the isolated gas molecules, respectively.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

The manuscript presents a study on a fluorine-doped carbon nitride (F-CN) photocatalyst for the selective reduction of NO to N2, demonstrating improved activity and selectivity. While the authors performed various characterizations and simulations to explore the structure–performance relationship, the actual role of the C–F bond in enhancing photocatalytic selectivity and activity remains insufficiently elucidated. Furthermore, the manuscript contains several conceptual inaccuracies and unsupported claims. I recommend a thorough revaluation of the experimental data and computational models to more accurately interpret the catalytic mechanism and correct the errors throughout the manuscript.
1. The central issue lies in the unclear interpretation of how C–F coordination affects the selectivity for N2. The authors emphasize that the inert nature of O2 contributes to high N2 selectivity. However, experimental data show that the N2 selectivity across all three catalysts remains nearly unchanged regardless of the presence of O2, even though the non-F-doped samples (e-OCN and e-CN) exhibit strong O2 adsorption. This contradicts the argument that weak O2 adsorption due to F doping is responsible for enhanced N2 selectivity. If O2 adsorption truly limited N2 selectivity, one would expect significantly lower selectivity in e-OCN and e-CN under O2-rich conditions. The authors should reconsider the mechanistic interpretation and provide a more convincing explanation.
2. The molecular models shown in Figure 1a appear to have incorrect bonding geometries. When F or O atoms are axially bonded to carbon, the coordination number of the carbon atom exceeds four, which violates basic valence rules. These structures need to be revised to reflect chemically plausible configurations, especially since they serve as the basis for DFT simulations.
3. The authors should report the catalyst’s surface temperature under light irradiation to determine whether the reaction is purely photocatalytic or has a significant photothermal component, especially considering the gas–solid phase setup. Additionally, isotopic labelling experiments (e.g., using 15NO) are necessary to confirm that the nitrogen in the evolved N2 originates from NO, not from decomposition of the catalyst itself.
4. To better understand the carrier dynamics and redox behaviour, the authors should conduct in situ XPS to trace the spatial distribution of photogenerated carriers, especially in e-FCN. Moreover, the band structures of all three catalysts should be experimentally determined (e.g., via UV-vis DRS, VB XPS, Mott–Schottky plots) to assess how F doping influences charge separation and redox potential—critical factors for selectivity.
5. How to exclude the O disturbance as I can see from XPS results that C-O-C bond exists in these three samples.
6. The data presented in Figure 5b must be normalized appropriately to enable valid comparisons among the three samples.
7. The rationale for including relative humidity (RH) in the reaction system is unclear. Does RH significantly impact the photocatalytic performance or selectivity? If so, the mechanism should be discussed. If not, the necessity of its inclusion should be justified.
8. The photocatalyst appears to exhibit deactivation after approximately three hours. The manuscript attributes this to NO3⁻ accumulation but provides no further evidence or mitigation strategy. The authors should explore the deactivation mechanism more thoroughly and suggest ways to minimize it, such as periodic regeneration.
9. In the 13C NMR spectrum of the e-CN sample, a noticeable shoulder peak is present. The authors should assign this peak and discuss whether it represents a unique carbon environment or a defect structure.
10. O2 adsorption capacity is only reported under dark conditions. Since light irradiation could influence surface charge and adsorption behaviour, the authors should also measure O2 adsorption under light to better understand its real-time interaction with the photocatalyst during operation.

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript addresses the significant challenge of photocatalytic selective NO decomposition to N2 under oxygen-rich conditions by introducing C-F bonds into the CN structure, developing an oxygen-tolerant e-FCN catalyst. The work achieves efficient photocatalytic NO-to-N2 conversion under oxygen-rich conditions, with experiments and theoretical calculations demonstrating that C-F bond engineering inhibits C=O bond formation to block O2 adsorption while selectively activating NO. This provides a novel strategy for designing oxygen-tolerant selective NO reduction catalysts. However, several concerns require clarification:
1.Are the C-F bonds functioning as isolated sites or synergistically with other functional groups (e.g., -NH₂)? Further clarification of the active center is necessary.
2.While in situ FTIR confirms NO consumption and N2 generation, the specific conversion pathway remains unclear. Time-resolved experiments or isotopic labeling should be incorporated to elucidate the dynamic NO transformation mechanism.
3. The study focuses exclusively on the carbon nitride system and TiO2-x as a reference but lacks comparisons with other fluorinated materials. This omission weakens the claim of the uniqueness of C-F bond modification.
4.High-temperature pyrolysis of NH4F may generate toxic byproducts (e.g., HF). A rigorous evaluation of the synthesis route’s environmental feasibility, including byproduct management and safety protocols, is strongly recommended.

### Reviewer 3

This manuscript reports the design and performance of a fluorine-modified polymeric carbon nitride photocatalyst for the selective reduction of NO to N₂ under oxygen-rich conditions. The authors claim a significant advance in achieving high N₂ selectivity and robust performance in the presence of O2. The work also proposes a mechanistic rationale for the observed selectivity. The manuscript is generally well written, the experimental procedures are detailed, and the supporting data are extensive. However, I have several comments regarding the novelty, evidence for the claims, and mechanistic interpretations.
1. The manuscript should explain more clearly how this method is different from recent work using TiO₂, metal oxides, or doped carbon nitrides. Also, compare both performance and mechanism with these methods.
2. The main claim is that C-F bonds help NO adsorption over O₂. The evidence comes mostly from TPD and DFT. Have the authors done direct surface tests with both gases together, like DRIFTS or co-adsorption?
3. Main results are shown for single runs with little error analysis. Did the authors repeat key tests? Can they provide error bars or confidence intervals for main results?
4. FTIR shows N₂O as a possible intermediate for N₂. Can the authors rule out other paths or surface nitrogen species? Is there isotopic data, like with ¹⁵NO, that tracks nitrogen atoms directly?
5. The authors claim better charge separation in e-FCN by F doping, using PL, TRPL, and EIS. These changes are moderate. Can they show transient absorption or time-resolved EPR data to link this to NO reduction?
6. The manuscript sometimes says "20% O₂ and Ar atmosphere," but other conditions are not clear. What is the NO concentration? Are conditions the same for all tests? Please add a summary table of all test conditions.
7. The method for tuning F content is not clear. How do the authors control F amount during synthesis? How do they confirm F content? Please describe the process and show data on F content and its reproducibility.
8. The authors say e-FCN is stable for 3 hours of use. What steps kept reaction conditions steady? Were there changes in temperature, humidity, or flow rates? Please explain operational stability and note any changes during the test.
9. The relation between electron density overlap and N–N bond comes from DFT and FTIR. More direct proof, like charge density plots or Bader analysis, would help. Can the authors explain how this overlap leads to N–N bonds?
10. EPR changes after EDTA are said to show O⁻ anions. Little change without EDTA means O⁻ reacts to make O₂. Can the authors show O₂ release directly or use isotopic tests? Also, provide more EPR details to separate signals.
Other minor issues:
The work needs a simple figure of electronic changes after F doping, like charge maps.
Tables S2 and S3: Make sure all cited values use the same NO levels and test conditions.
Move key supporting data (like Table S1, Figures S6-7) into the main text for clarity.
State if F content stays the same after long testing, or if any F is lost.

### Reviewer 4

The manuscript presents an intriguing strategy for achieving selective photocatalytic reduction of nitric oxide to dinitrogen under oxygen-rich conditions using a fluorine-modified polymeric carbon nitride. The authors claim high performance performance metrics in terms of NO conversion efficiency and N₂ selectivity. The study is well-structured and uses a broad array of experimental and theoretical tools. However, several major concerns need to be addressed to justify the significance and robustness of the claims.
1. Comparative benchmarking is lacking for such a big claim as ‘first successful…). How does the performance quantitatively compare against other recent reports and what features distinguish the current work compared to literature (AQY, RH conditions, loading etc.)?
2. The tests are performed at 20% O₂ under dry conditions. However, this does not fully simulate ambient air given that indoor environments possess varying humidity and gases. Authors must add additional data (or at least discuss) photocatalytic performance under variable RH (20–60%) and presence of NO₂, SO₂, or CO₂.
3. The mass balance assumes equimolar N₂ and O₂ formation without direct quantification of oxygen evolution in all cases. Authors must provide full molar balances for N-containing species. Is there any undetected nitrogen retained on the catalyst surface?
4. The proposed mechanism is plausible, but the assignment of FTIR peaks to this species is speculative which must be supported with isotope labeling experiments.
5. The study shows stability over 6 cycles, but NO₃⁻ accumulation must be quantified per cycle and authors should aim for higher stability demonstration beyond 6 cycles (e.g., 10–15) to assess long-term operational efficacy.
6. In this work, the reactor uses artificial gas mixtures. However, ambient conditions often include fluctuating light, temperature and humidity. Such experiments must be provided to pave the way towards real indoor applications.
7. Data on exfoliation, particle size and morphology (change) on each modification step must be provided.
8. Eventhough it is common in photocatalysis field to show results obtained from single experiment, average results with error bars obtained from minimum 3 experiments (especially on identifying selectivity) can improve reliability of data.
9. Time-resolved PL data were collected under ambient conditions but can charge carrier dynamics be examined under photocatalytic reaction conditions (e.g., in NO/O₂/Ar atmospheres) to better reflect catalytic behavior under given experimental condition.
10. In some places it is mentioned that increased NO adsorption on e-FCN based on TPD and FTIR results, but is it possible to quantify surface coverage of NO and O₂ (in µmol/m²) to assess catalyst efficiency per site?
11. The bandgap of e-FCN is given, but band positions relative to NO reduction potential are not clearly shown. Flat band potential and/or valence/conduction band positions must be given and compared to NO/N₂O/N₂ redox potentials?
12. Could water displace NO from active sites through adsorption?
13. Exfoliation is said to weaken π–π interactions resulting in improved performance, but is there a method/data to prove the claim?
14. Time-resolved PL data were collected under ambient conditions but can charge carrier dynamics be examined under photocatalytic reaction conditions (e.g., in NO/O₂/Ar atmospheres) to better reflect catalytic behavior under given experimental condition.

## Round 1 — Authors' Response

Response Letter
Reviewer 1's Comments:
The manuscript presents a study on a fluorine-doped carbon nitride (F-CN) photocatalyst for the selective reduction of NO to N , demonstrating improved activity and selectivity. While the authors performed various characterizations and simulations to explore the structure-performance relationship, the actual role of the C-F bond in enhancing photocatalytic selectivity and activity remains insufficiently elucidated. Furthermore, the manuscript contains several conceptual inaccuracies and unsupported claims. I recommend a thorough revaluation of the experimental data and computational models to more accurately interpret the catalytic mechanism and correct the errors throughout the manuscript.
Comment 1: The central issue lies in the unclear interpretation of how C-F coordination affects the selectivity for N . The authors emphasize that the inert nature of O contributes to high N selectivity. However, experimental data show that the N selectivity across all three catalysts remains nearly unchanged regardless of the presence of O , even though the non-F-doped samples (e-OCN and e-CN) exhibit strong O adsorption. This contradicts the argument that weak O adsorption due to F doping is responsible for enhanced N selectivity. If O adsorption truly limited N selectivity, one would expect significantly lower selectivity in e-OCN and e-CN under O -rich conditions. The authors should reconsider the mechanistic interpretation and provide a more convincing explanation.
Response 1: We have elucidated the similar N selectivity observed for the e-CN, e-OCN, and e-FCN catalysts under both Ar and 20% O /Ar atmospheres.

Under the Ar atmosphere, e-CN, e-OCN, and e-FCN all underwent photocatalytic NO decomposition, producing N O as a byproduct. In contrast, under the 20% O /Ar atmosphere, the catalysts displayed distinct behaviors: e-FCN remained primarily governed by NO decomposition, with minimal NO oxidation, resulting in comparable N selectivity in both conditions. However, as shown in Figure 2A, e-CN and e-OCN generated substantially more NO - than N O, indicating a predominant photocatalytic oxidation pathway (converting NO to NO -) rather than decomposition. Reviewer 3's Comments:
This manuscript reports the design and performance of a fluorine-modified polymeric carbon nitride photocatalyst for the selective reduction of NO to N under oxygen-rich conditions. The 2 authors claim a significant advance in achieving high N selectivity and robust performance in the 2 presence of O . The work also proposes a mechanistic rationale for the observed selectivity. The 2 manuscript is generally well written, the experimental procedures are detailed, and the supporting data are extensive. However, I have several comments regarding the novelty, evidence for the claims, and mechanistic interpretations.
Comment 1: The manuscript should explain more clearly how this method is different from recent work using mp-TiO , metal oxides, or doped carbon nitrides. Also, compare both performance 2-x and mechanism with these methods.
Response 1: We delineated the distinctions between e-FCN and previously reported systems for photocatalytic NO removal.
(p3-4) “While the photocatalytic oxidation of NO to NO - is well-established,22 achieving its 3 selective reduction to N without a chemical reductant in oxygen-rich environments remains 2 challenging.25 We demonstrated a breakthrough: the oxygen-tolerant, selective photoreduction of NO to N under visible light irradiation.” 2
Additionally, a comparative analysis of its catalytic performance against relevant benchmarks for photocatalytic NO decomposition was conducted.
(p10-11)
“To evaluate the uniqueness of the proposed C-F modification strategy, we systematically compared the performance of several catalysts under both Ar and 20% O /Ar atmospheres. The 2 tested catalysts included: e-FCN (containing C-F bonds), our previously developed mp-TiO ,25 2-x surface-fluorinated F-mp-TiO 48 and the BiOBr/BiOF system featuring O-Br/F bonds49. As 2-x shown in Figures 3A-B, e-FCN exhibited superior catalytic performance under both conditions. Notably, while mp-TiO demonstrated activity comparable to e-FCN in an Ar atmosphere, its NO 2-x removal efficiency and N selectivity decreased significantly in 20% O /Ar, with substantial NO 2 2 2 byproduct formation. Further analysis revealed that surface F doping (F-mp-TiO ) slightly 2-x improved NO removal efficiency but increased NO generation, suggesting that surface F doping 2 primarily promotes the undesired oxidation of NO to NO rather than NO decomposition under 2 oxygen-rich conditions. Similarly, the BiOF system (containing O-F bonds) showed marginally higher activity than BiOBr but remained ineffective for NO decomposition in an oxygen-rich environment. These comparative results clearly demonstrate the distinct advantage of the C-F modification strategy in developing highly efficient NO decomposition catalysts.
Although photocatalytic processes for NO removal have been extensively studied,22 the majority of prior research has focused on the selective oxidation of NO to NO -. We recently employed mp- 3 TiO to achieve selective NO reduction to N without chemical reductant in anoxic condition but 2-x 2 its performance was drastically reduced in the presence of O .25 In contrast, e-FCN demonstrated 2 superior efficiency in converting NO to N across a range of NO concentrations (0.5-2.0 ppmv; 2 see Figure 3C) and the concentration of O had a negligible effect on both NO removal efficiency 2 and N selectivity (Figure 3D). Conversely, oxygen-modified CN (e-OCN) promoted NO 2 oxidation to NO - in the presence of O (Figure S11), shifting the primary byproduct from N O to 3 2 2 NO - as O concentration increased from 0% to 20%. This behavior starkly contrasts with F- 3 2 modified CN (e-FCN), which enables oxygen-tolerant NO decomposition to N regardless of O 2 2 presence. As listed in Tables S3-4, the photocatalytic performance and AQYs of e-FCN in NO decomposition under 20% O exceed those of previously reported catalysts, even at an initial NO 2 concentration as low as 0.5 ppmv.”

Reviewer 4's Comments:
The manuscript presents an intriguing strategy for achieving selective photocatalytic reduction of nitric oxide to dinitrogen under oxygen-rich conditions using a fluorine-modified polymeric carbon nitride. The authors claim high performance metrics in terms of NO conversion efficiency and N selectivity. The study is well-structured and uses a broad array of experimental and 2 theoretical tools. However, several major concerns need to be addressed to justify the significance and robustness of the claims.
Comment 1: Comparative benchmarking is lacking for such a big claim as ‘first successful…). How does the performance quantitatively compare against other recent reports and what features distinguish the current work compared to literature (AQY, RH conditions, loading etc.)?
Response 1: We delineated the distinctions between e-FCN and previously reported systems for photocatalytic NO removal.
(p3-4) “While the photocatalytic oxidation of NO to NO - is well-established,22 achieving its 3 selective reduction to N without a chemical reductant in oxygen-rich environments remains 2 challenging.25 We demonstrated a breakthrough: the oxygen-tolerant, selective photoreduction of NO to N under visible light irradiation.” 2
Comment 2: The tests are performed at 20% O under dry conditions. However, this does not fully 2 simulate ambient air given that indoor environments possess varying humidity and gases. Authors must add additional data (or at least discuss) photocatalytic performance under variable RH (20- 60%) and presence of NO , SO , or CO .
Response 2: The effects of CO , NO , and SO on the photocatalytic NO decomposition were 2 2 2 systematically examined to evaluate the performance of an e-FCN catalyst under practical indoor conditions.
(p13-14) “In practical indoor environments, air contains a certain level of relative humidity (RH), and NO pollutants often coexist with other gases, such as CO , NO , and SO .51 It is therefore 2 2 2 essential to evaluate the effects of RH and coexisting gases on photocatalytic NO decomposition over e-FCN. Figures S15-16 systematically examined these influences by testing e-FCN under common indoor RH levels and typical concentration ratios of NO to CO , NO , and SO . Figure 2 2 2 S15 indicated that RH has a minor effect on photocatalytic NO decomposition, suggesting that H O molecules do not significantly compete with NO for adsorption and activation sites on the 2 catalyst surface. Similarly, coexisting CO exhibited a negligible impact (Figure S16A-B). This 2 observation aligns with prior theoretical calculations indicating that the adsorption energy of NO on F-CN is significantly more favorable than that of CO , leading to the preferential adsorption of 2 NO.32 To evaluate the effect of NO , the total initial NO concentration was maintained at 2.0 ppmv 2 x while varying the NO proportion. The results indicate that neither the NO removal efficiency nor 2 x the N selectivity was significantly affected (Figures S16C-D). Furthermore, no NO was detected 2 2 in the effluent. In this study, the initial NO concentration exceeded that of the coexisting NO . 2 x Under these conditions, the two species primarily reacted via the fast SCR pathway in a 1:1 molar ratio, forming the unstable intermediate N O .52 This intermediate was then rapidly reduced by 2 3 photogenerated electrons. This reaction pathway explains the absence of NO in the effluent. The 2 presence of SO slightly inhibited the photocatalytic decomposition of NO (Figures S16E-F). This 2 inhibition can be attributed to SO acting as a scavenger for photogenerated holes, a mechanism 2 previously documented in aqueous reaction systems.53 The consumption of holes by SO disrupts 2 the charge balance within the photocatalytic system, thereby altering the pathway for NO decomposition.”

(p23-25)
“The NO/O adsorption results demonstrate that the presence of the C-F bond in CN suppresses 2 the formation of the C=O bond, rendering e-FCN inert towards O . To investigate the NO 2 photoconversion process in the presence of O , in-situ FTIR spectroscopy was employed to 2 monitor the chemical transformation process. The FTIR spectra of initial NO adsorption on e-CN, e-OCN, and e-FCN reveal distinct bands (Figure S27): one at 1690-1694 cm-1, corresponding to adsorbed (NO) species on the surface,68 and others at 1273 and 1411-1413 cm-1, indicative of 2 bridged (NO) species.17 These bands (1273, 1411-1413, and 1694 cm-1) increase gradually over 2 time (Figures S27A, C, E), and e-FCN consistently exhibits higher band intensities compared with e-CN and e-OCN, thereby confirming stronger NO binding on e-FCN (Figures S27B, D, F). The signals at 1273 and 1411-1413 cm-1 are typically attributed to the symmetric vibration of bridging bidentate NO -.69 However, the absence of corresponding signals for asymmetric vibrations in the 3 higher wavenumber range (1500-1700 cm-1) challenges this interpretation. Based on these spectral features, we attribute these two bands to the presence of a bridged (NO) dimer adsorbed onto the 2 catalysts.
The assignment of the observed feature to an (NO) dimer was confirmed unequivocally using 2 15NO isotope-substituted in-situ FTIR spectroscopy. As shown in Figure S28, the spectrum exhibited a corresponding redshift to lower wavenumber. The experimental ν(15N)/ν(N) ratios showed excellent agreement with theoretical values predicted for an (NO) dimer (Table S12), 2 thereby confirming this assignment.70 Complementary DFT calculations were employed to investigate NO adsorption behavior and co-adsorbed NO interactions on the e-FCN surface. One or two NO molecules were introduced onto the e-FCN surface slab (Figures 6C-F). Computed adsorption energies revealed a more stable configuration for the (NONO) dimer, with a total E (NONO) of -0.31 eV for the dimer system, compared with E (NO) = -0.21 eV for a single ads ads NO molecule (Figures 6C-D). This enhanced stability arises from both π back-donation to the NO ligands and direct attractive interactions between the co-adsorbed NO molecules. Charge density analysis indicated significant electron accumulation at the adsorption sites, increasing from 0.36 |e| for a single NO molecule to 0.69 |e| for the dimer system (Figures 6E-F), consistent with enhanced electron transfer from the e-FCN substrate. The total charge associated with the dimer was less than the sum of the two isolated NO adsorbates. This charge redistribution, combined with the adjacent geometry of the two N atoms, suggests a mechanism that mitigates inter- adsorbate repulsion and facilitates N-N coupling. The assignment of vibrational bands to an (NO) 2 dimer, confirmed through in-situ isotopic FTIR and theoretical calculations, indicates that N-N bond formation occurs via a partial overlap of electron density between adjacent N atoms.25

These results highlight the critical role of e-FCN in promoting the photocatalytic reduction of N O intermediates to N . 2 2 Notably, a band at 1555 cm-1 was observed for all catalysts under light irradiation (Figures S29A, C, E), indicating the accumulation of bidentate NO - on the catalyst surface.73 Among the catalysts, 3 e-OCN exhibits the highest NO - accumulation. This finding is consistent with the observation that 3 NO - selectivity for e-OCN is higher than that for e-CN and e-FCN (see above Figure 2A). 3
Definitive confirmation of the N O and NO - feature assignments was achieved using 15NO 2 3 isotope-substituted in-situ FTIR spectroscopy. This study analyzes the dynamic behavior of surface species by tracking the temporal evolution of their characteristic FTIR peak areas. Consequently, the analysis is restricted to relative comparisons of concentration changes on a single catalyst and precludes quantitative comparisons of peak intensities between different catalysts. This approach therefore does not necessitate strictly quantitative intensity measurements.

Comment 13: Exfoliation is said to weaken π-π interactions resulting in improved performance, but is there a method/data to prove the claim?
Response 13: The enhancement of exfoliation facilitated by electron-withdrawing O and F was elucidated initially.
(p5) “Both AFM and DLS revealed a consistent exfoliation trend across the catalyst series. AFM measurements indicated that the particle thickness decreased in the order (Figure S2): e-CN (4.3- 4.9 nm) > e-OCN (2.8-3.4 nm) > e-FCN (2.3-2.7 nm). This trend was corroborated by DLS, which showed a corresponding decrease in hydrodynamic diameter (Figure S3): e-CN (133.1 ± 1.7 nm) > e-OCN (122.7 ± 1.3 nm) > e-FCN (110.6 ± 1.1 nm). Charge distribution calculations confirmed the strong electron-withdrawing nature of the O and F atoms, which generated a highly positive C center (Figure S4). The greater electronegativity of F resulted in a more positive charge on this C center in the FCN model (+1.81) compared with that in the OCN model (+1.70). We therefore propose that this electron-withdrawing effect is the primary driver of enhanced exfoliation. The incorporation of O or F into the CN matrix attenuates the interlayer π-π interactions, thereby facilitating delamination. The superior efficacy of F stems directly from its higher electronegativity, which more effectively disrupts these cohesive forces and promotes exfoliation.”
Figure S4D, F. Charge distribution of the (D) e-OCN and (F) e-FCN. The C, N, H, O, and F atoms are represented by dark grey, white, pink, red, and cyan spheres.
The BET surface areas and pore volumes of the catalysts were subsequently compared.
(p19) “As summarized in Table S10, the Brunauer-Emmett-Teller (BET) surface area and pore volume increase in the order: e-CN < e-OCN < e-FCN. The preceding AFM and DLS analyses confirmed the successful exfoliation of the CN-based catalysts (Figures S2-3). The introduction of electronegative O and F atoms effectively weakened the interlayer π-π interactions, thereby facilitating exfoliation. Owing to its higher electronegativity, F exerted a more pronounced effect, as evidenced by the decreasing order of both average particle thickness and average hydrodynamic particle size: e-CN > e-OCN > e-FCN. For layered materials, the specific surface area is primarily governed by the exposed surfaces of the exfoliated nanosheets. Theoretically, greater exfoliation reduces both the average number of layers and the overall thickness, resulting in a larger specific surface area.36 The observed BET surface area and pore volume trend aligns well with this principle.”
Finally, the catalytic performance of the bulk and exfoliated catalysts was compared, demonstrating that exfoliation enhances catalytic performance.
(p19) “To evaluate the influence of exfoliation on photocatalytic NO decomposition activity, bulk CN-based photocatalysts were also prepared and tested as control samples under the identical reaction conditions. As illustrated in Figures S24A-D, the photocatalytic NO removal efficiency and N selectivity of the bulk catalysts were significantly lower than those of the exfoliated 2 catalysts in both Ar and 20% O . The surface area and pore volume of the bulk catalysts are 2 substantially smaller than those of the exfoliated catalysts (Figures S23A-B and Table S10). This suggests that exfoliation increases the number of active sites exposed on the catalyst surface, thereby enhancing NO adsorption and subsequent activation.36”
